insights.headline: She protects her family's functional stability by solving crises alone and controlling the narrative they receive, while framing this as pragmatism rather than protection.
insights.explanation: E1: At 14, during financial collapse, she invents an inventory system and game ('Operation Manage') without being asked, managing her siblings' knowledge. She tells Bisola a euphemism ('Daddy is changing business') she marks as untrue (L42: 'Which, you know'). Stated frame: learning to prioritize material reality (L63-65: 'Not how do I feel about it'). Lived pattern: she solves problems alone to protect others from knowledge or obligation. E2: When her father is acutely ill, she avoids calling Aunty Funmi—who would solve fastest—because she knows it creates one year of relational debt (L39: 'every conversation will have that inside it'). She solves it herself instead, using her allowance and her mother's hidden resources (L41-42). E5: She plans emigration in secret (L17: 'I have not told one single person in my family'), controlling when and how her family learns about it. Why? 'the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for' (L24-25). The gap: she says she is pragmatic; she is actually bearing family crises alone to protect others from shame or burden.

evidence.quote: I said no, Daddy is changing business. Which, you know. He was changing business.

I knew what would happen — she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it. Every single one. So I called my coursemate Kemi whose uncle is at a private hospital in Ogba, and I did the referral myself, and I took my whole allowance from the placement.

I can't bring it to the table until I know. Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for. You understand? Five people are disappointed instead of one.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Relationships: She will take on financial or logistical labour without disclosing the weight, and experience resentment when her partner does not perceive the work. She will resist being helped because help creates obligation she cannot reciprocate.

insights.headline: She believes that if she makes her needs, hopes or labour visible, she becomes a burden and distributes failure to others; therefore she must solve problems alone and pre-emptively.
insights.explanation: E1 (age 14): During financial collapse, she invents an inventory and game without being asked and without telling anyone. The behaviour implies: her distress would add to her parents' distress, so she protects by managing silently. E2 (age 19): When her father is acutely ill, she deliberately avoids calling Aunty Funmi because the money will create relational debt ('for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it,' L39-40). The belief: if I ask for help, I become a problem someone else has to solve. E5 (age 24): She plans emigration in complete secrecy, calculating costs in three scenarios (L12-16). She will not disclose 'until I know' (L23). Why? 'Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for' (L24-26). This is explicit: she believes making her hopes visible distributes failure to others, making her responsible for their disappointment. The underlying belief: my visibility costs others.

evidence.quote: I knew what would happen — she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it. Every single one. So I called my coursemate Kemi.

I can't bring it to the table until I know. Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for. You understand? Five people are disappointed instead of one. When I have the CBT pass in my hand, then I'll say it.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Personal Growth: She will not disclose setbacks or failures to close family until she has 'fixed' them or moved past them. If forced to disclose before ready, she will experience shame or sense that she has burdened others, even if they express support.

insights.headline: She excels at seeing a system's constraints, designing structures that create agency in others within those constraints, and executing the solution alone without external validation.
insights.explanation: E1 (age 14): Without being asked, she enters a storage room, invents a taxonomy (Item, Quantity, Days to Depletion), calculates food consumption for seven people, and projects depletion dates. She then converts this data into a game ('Operation Manage') that makes her siblings active participants in scarcity management without external resources (the reward is choosing Sunday viewing, which requires no cost). She is energized by this work ('something in my chest go down,' L34). E3 (age 17-18): After failing medicine, she recognizes that nursing offers transparent structure ('when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything,' L41). She goes to a cyber café and changes her course herself, paying with her own money, telling no one (L42-44). E5 (age 24): She works out the exact visa and licensing pathway from the NMC website, calculates costs in three scenarios with currency fluctuation, determines the salary she needs, and reverse-engineers a contribution plan: 'I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month comfortably. Which handles Tayo completely and starts a pool for Bisola' (L40-41). This is not daydreaming; it is systems design that creates agency for her siblings through her own structure.

evidence.quote: I told them we were doing a competition. I called it Operation Manage. Whoever wastes the least food in a week gets to choose what we watch on Sunday.

When I got the handbook in first year and I saw the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel. My roommate was laughing at me. But you know what that is, that's — when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Work and Career: In a role with undefined structure, she will quickly map constraints and design a system without being asked. She will implement it. Others will recognize it as elegant. She may become the person others 'ask how to do things,' but may not receive formal credit.

insights.headline: She maintains precise, indexed memories of others' behaviour (dates, durations, objects), while simultaneously disclaiming she is tracking, and this data appears to function as a measure of care received.
insights.explanation: E1: She states 'I am not a person that keeps record of what people did' (L52), then immediately contradicts: 'That's just how my head is' (L60), and provides precise indexing: Uncle Segun came 'September and then just before Christmas,' dated to 'the 14th of September because it was after my birthday' (L54, L61). She recalls a one-hour-twenty-minute car negotiation (L47) and can 'spell demurrage backwards' (L11). E4: She states 'I don't get attached, that's the thing about me, I think I'm actually quite hard in that way' (L48), yet she remembers the son's shoes ('nice shoes... the kind that makes that sound on the floor,' L7) and recalls the absence as exactly 'nineteen days' (L14-15, repeated: 'I know it was nineteen because I know,' L17). She carries Mama Ronke's comb 'since last year' (L50-52). She tells the son 'she was comfortable,' but also states 'I remember what date he last came before that, and I remember what the shoes sounded like' (L60). Pattern: she collects precise data about who showed up, when, and what they brought. She measures relational care through this data, then denies she is doing so. Question: Does she believe acknowledging she is tracking means admitting she is keeping score (which feels disloyal)? Or does tracking feel like the only form of witnessing available to her?

evidence.quote: The only one that came to the house that whole time was Uncle Segun, and he came twice, September and then just before Christmas, and the second time he brought a bag of rice and a crate of egg and he didn't even come inside, he dropped it at the gate.
I will tell you that I remember what date he last came before that, and I remember what the shoes sounded like. I don't know why my head keeps those things. It's not useful.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Relationships: In a close relationship, she will notice and remember small failures to show up (partner forgetting a detail, late arrival). She will accumulate this data without naming it. When the relationship cracks, she will produce this data as evidence of neglect, and the other person will be shocked because the data was never surfaced. She will experience herself as 'just stating facts' while the other experiences her as 'keeping score.'

insights.headline: She describes herself as analytical and pragmatic, but her major decisions emerge from bodily knowing or ambient sensing, executed first and rationalized after.
insights.explanation: E3: She is deciding between rewriting JAMB, changing courses, or paying for private medicine (high-stakes, rational choice). She states explicitly: 'I didn't reason it. I want to be clear, there was no reasoning. It was like somebody came and put it in my hand' (L29-31). The trigger: watching a woman sell gala in rain with wet hands. 'My mind just — it went quiet. And I said, nursing. Just like that... I didn't reason it' (L24-29). Then after: 'Then after, I built all the reasons. Oh, nursing is four to five years not seven...' (L32-38). Post-hoc rationalization. She states: 'I tell them I'm a very analytical person' (L59), but admits 'That's how most of my big things have gone, if I'm honest. Which I don't tell people because it sounds mad' (E3 L57-58). E5: She is making a second major decision (emigration, hidden from family). She says: 'I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it' (L52-53). She has done cost analysis and NMC research, but the final decision will not be rational. It will emerge from her body, as with nursing.

evidence.quote: Some days I'm reading the NMC page and I'm calm, everything is steps, do step one do step two. Other days I'm thinking, if I leave, who is the one that will be at the house when my daddy's BP does that thing again. Who will count what is remaining. I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Personal Growth: When deliberately trying to think through a decision, analysis will stall her. She is more likely to find clarity through situations that trigger bodily response (walking, crisis, ambient sensing). If she relies on analytical mind as primary tool, she will experience cycles of overthinking without resolution.

insights.headline: By E5, she has moved from absorbing her family's crisis (inventory at 14) to pre-emptively architecting her life to become her family's financial solution (emigration plan at 24), suggesting she may believe this is now inevitable.
insights.explanation: E1 (age 14): Crisis arrives; she responds by counting, organizing, managing siblings' knowledge. Reactive but extraordinary. E2 (age 19): Someone else (Aunty Funmi) is the financial solution; she resists dependency on that role. E3 (age 17-18): She commits to nursing, a care profession with 'a licence with a number,' transparency, predictability. E4 (age 23): In clinical work, she performs care labour beyond duty (plaiting hair, mouth care, talking to dead patient), despite Sister Adaeze saying she is doing too much. E5 (age 24): She has calculated that on a UK nurse salary, 'I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month comfortably. Which handles Tayo completely and starts a pool for Bisola' (L40-41). She is not emigrating for herself; she is emigrating to become the financial solution for four siblings. She states: 'That's the whole thing. That's the actual reason' (L42-43). The compounding insight: she has internalized the role of crisis-absorber, refused to be dependent, chosen a care profession, practiced it beyond requirement, and now is architecting her life around funding her siblings' education. The logic is: if I am the one who manages, I must become the one who solves. This is only visible because E5 shows the trajectory completing—she is not just managing a crisis, she is building her life around preventing future crises for her family.

evidence.quote: I was turning her two-hourly with whoever I could grab. I plaited her hair one night because it was matting and I couldn't — it was disturbing me. Not for her, she didn't know. For me.

My mummy would be happy, honestly, half of Lagos wants their child in UK. Aunty Funmi would probably pay for the CBT on the spot, she'd be telling her prayer group the same week. It's just — I can't. I can't bring it to the table until I know.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Purpose: If emigration succeeds, she will experience it not as freedom but as responsibility. She will send money and experience recurring anxiety about what is happening at home without her. She will not 'move abroad' in the sense of building a life there; she will build a life structured around remote family management. She may burn out or achieve success while experiencing emptiness, because she moved to solve a family problem that individual earning cannot solve.

insights.headline: She believes that if a system or path is transparent and rule-based (step one, step two, step three leads to outcome), then she can navigate it alone and without dependency or the need for connections.
insights.explanation: E1: She is facing a financial crisis with no transparent outcome. She invents transparency: 'Item, Quantity, How many days it can carry us' (L27-29). This makes the crisis predictable and manageable. E3: She faced opaque paths to medicine (rewrite, change course, private university)—all involving gatekeeping and 'knowing somebody.' Nursing offers a different path: 'you do your programme, you do your indexing, you register with the Nursing and Midwifery Council, you have a licence with a number. There is a syllabus. Nobody can come and say ah your uncle knows so-and-so' (L35-37). This is the actual reason she chose it. She states: 'when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything' (L41). E4: In clinical work, last offices has a transparent protocol: 'there is an order. First this, then this' (L44-45). She executes it with precision and steadiness. E5: She maps the emigration pathway step by step: 'CBT, then application, then qualification verification, then OSCE, then the OSCE is in the UK so you need the visa, which means you need the job offer, which means the sponsorship' (L12-13). This belief permits her to navigate systems alone because she does not need to ask anyone or know anyone; she just needs to see the steps. The system is the permission.

evidence.quote: When we did the last offices, Sister Adaeze took me through it. And there is a way you do it. You wash the body, you position it, you pack with cotton wool, you remove the cannula and the catheter, you do the identification, you write the tag, you record the time on the chart. There is an order. First this, then this.

I opened the NMC website and I wrote out the whole thing in my book. CBT, then application, then qualification verification, then OSCE, then the OSCE is in the UK so you need the visa, which means you need the job offer, which means the sponsorship...

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Work and Career: She will gravitate toward roles with clear hierarchies, written protocols, transparent progression (healthcare, civil service, structured finance). She will excel in these contexts. She may struggle in roles requiring political navigation or relationship-building. She will document and systematize processes others leave informal.

insights.headline: She values the capacity to act independently and avoid creating obligation or indebtedness in others; she will sacrifice convenience, comfort, or speed to protect this autonomy.
insights.explanation: E2: Her father is acutely ill. Aunty Funmi would solve fastest. But the speaker refuses to call her because 'she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it' (L39-40). She chooses a slower, harder path: calling a coursemate's uncle for a referral, using her allowance, asking her mother to sell something. The cost: possible worse health outcome, family humiliation, sacrificed allowance. The value protected: independence, no debt to Aunty. E5: She could ask for help paying for IELTS or CBT. Aunty would 'probably pay for the CBT on the spot' (L21). But she refuses because 'the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for' (L24-25). She sacrifices comfort (secret keeping, anxiety) and safety (no one knows where she is going) to protect autonomy. E1: She could tell her parents what she has discovered. She could ask for help. Instead, she manages alone, creating a game that protects her siblings from the truth. The cost: she bears the knowledge and responsibility alone. The value: no one is burdened by her understanding; she solves.

evidence.quote: I knew what would happen — she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it. Every single one. So I called my coursemate Kemi whose uncle is at a private hospital in Ogba, and I did the referral myself, and I took my whole allowance from the placement, and my mummy sold — well. We sorted it.

My mummy would be happy, honestly, half of Lagos wants their child in UK. Aunty Funmi would probably pay for the CBT on the spot, she'd be telling her prayer group the same week. It's just — I can't. I can't bring it to the table until I know.

insights.would_predict: PILLAR: Relationships: She will be reluctant to ask for emotional support, financial help, or practical assistance, and will solve alone or seek solutions outside the partnership. The partner may experience this as rejection or distance. She may experience the partner's offer to help as an obligation incurred, and will work to 'repay' it, creating an exhausting cycle. She may be drawn to partners who are also independent, creating emotional isolation.

facts.what_happened: In 2016, when the speaker was fourteen years old, something significant occurred that she returns to repeatedly.
The speaker's father was importing generators (Tiger, Elepaq brands) and tyres; he had two shipping containers at Apapa port during the year the naira devalued sharply against the dollar.
Port demurrage fees accumulated; the speaker learned the words 'demurrage' and 'restructuring' that year.
The father would return from Apapa, sit in a cane chair in the dark living room holding the television remote without turning it on. They had stopped buying diesel for the generator by June.
Daily greetings between speaker and father consisted of: 'e kaale sir' / 'how was school' / 'fine sir'—the same exchange for approximately four months.

The speaker went to the storage room, counted all food items (rice, garri, tinned tomatoes) in an exercise book, calculated daily consumption rates for seven people, and projected depletion dates for each item.

Younger siblings (Tayo, Bisola) asked if the family was moving or changing schools; the speaker created 'Operation Manage'—a competition for minimal food waste with Sunday television viewing as the stated prize.
When Bisola asked directly if father's business had failed, the speaker said no, that he was 'changing business.'
The father sold a Peugeot 504. A man from Ikorodu negotiated for one hour twenty minutes, then paid in cash from a black plastic bag; the father counted the money standing in the sun.
The neighbor's daughter (SS3 student) became pregnant that year and was moved to the village; the speaker's mother preached about it for two years afterward.
Of the father's three brothers, only Uncle Segun visited twice (September and just before Christmas); on the second visit he left rice and eggs at the gate without entering.

candidates.headline: She protects her family's dignity and functional stability by absorbing uncertainty herself rather than distributing panic.
candidates.explanation: When siblings asked existential questions about moving or changing schools (L36), the speaker created a false game rather than admit crisis. When Bisola asked if the business failed (L41), she reframed it as 'changing business'—a euphemism the speaker herself marks with 'Which, you know' (L42), showing she knew it was untrue but chose the lie anyway. This is not conflict avoidance; it is active structural work. She chose to inventory food (L25, unprompted), calculated depletion dates, and controlled the narrative her siblings received. The cost: she bore the knowledge alone and made deliberate false statements to people she cared for. The falsifier would be: 'I told them the truth about what was happening.' Her stated frame is that she learned to prioritize material reality over emotion (L63-L65), but the actual choice was to prioritize her siblings' stability over their right to accurate information.

She then performs a preemptive absolution: 'I am not a person that keeps record of what people did... Family is family' (L52-L53) and 'it's not that I'm holding anything' (L58). This is not genuine forgiveness; it is a belief stated as fact. She even proves she *does* keep records—she knows the exact dates (L54, L61)—yet frames her own record-keeping as involuntary ('That's just how my head is,' L60). The alternative reading: she expects abandonment, sees it happen, then erases the expectation to avoid the disappointment. She demonstrates this again in her elaborate defense of Uncle Kunle (L57): she did unpaid work for his daughter's event to prove she holds no grudge—a performance of forgiveness for an absence she did record. The absence: no reflection on whether she *should* hold the uncles accountable, or what their absence cost her father.
candidates.narrator_frame: L52-L53: 'I am not a person that keeps record of what people did, you know, I'm not. Family is family.' And L60: 'That's just how my head is.'

facts.what_happened: Aunty Funmi is the speaker's mother's immediate elder sister.
Aunty Funmi pays the speaker's school fees.
Aunty Funmi lives in Magodo; her husband works in oil and gas servicing; they have two children in Canada, one doing a master's degree.
The house has two generators, one for the house and one for the borehole.
There is a dog named Bingo at the house who the speaker says dislikes them specifically.
The speaker's mother took them to Aunty Funmi's house on a Saturday morning after receiving nursing school admission; they waited in the car for approximately two hours while Aunty was on a call.
Aunty Funmi hugged the speaker, called them 'Temi the doctor,' and said not to worry about fees.
Aunty Funmi paid school fees and accommodation every session, bought an HP laptop in the speaker's second year, and replaced a stolen stethoscope the same week.
The speaker keeps receipts and transfer alerts in a brown envelope in their box.
The speaker calls Aunty Funmi every Sunday evening after church and sends photographed results each semester; if results aren't sent within two days, Aunty calls the speaker's mother.
During holidays the speaker stays at Magodo and supervises workmen repairs, goes to market, and cooks for Aunty's prayer group.
In 2022, the speaker's father had a health episode at home where his speech was affected for approximately forty minutes then returned to normal.

The speaker did not call Aunty Funmi about the father's health incident; instead contacted a coursemate Kemi to arrange a referral to a private hospital in Ogba, used their own allowance from placement, and the mother contributed; the total cost was approximately eighty thousand naira.
After the father was stable and discharged, the speaker called Aunty Funmi and told her; Aunty responded angrily, asking why she wasn't called, and sent two hundred thousand naira that same night.
When the speaker's mother's freezer broke, Aunty Funmi bought her a replacement.
Aunty Funmi is coming to the speaker's graduation and has asked about aso-ebi colours.

Patient in bed seven was named Mama Ronke, age 68, admitted with CVA (cerebrovascular accident) and dense hemiplegia, aphasic, could speak approximately three words including water
Mama Ronke's son brought her in, paid the deposit and arranged investigations

Speaker performed mouth care on Mama Ronke every night, turned her two-hourly with other staff, plaited her hair one night, and talked to her regularly
Sister Adaeze told the speaker she was doing too much care for one patient when she had six others
Mama Ronke died on a Thursday at approximately 4:50 a.m.; speaker was present; breathing changed and then ceased

Sister Adaeze guided speaker through last offices procedure: washing the body, positioning, packing with cotton wool, removing cannula and catheter, identification, tagging, recording time on chart, in that specific order
During last offices, speaker's hands were steady and mind clear; afterwards sat on changing room bench and felt fine
Speaker has kept Mama Ronke's small black comb in her bag since the previous year
The son came on Friday, was crying, speaker took him to office, gave him water, told him the patient was comfortable, he thanked her and said God bless you, she responded it's okay sir

Kemi drove the speaker to the IELTS exam.

CGE results are due in less than four months, followed by indexing, licensing, and an internship.

candidates.headline: She protects her family's functional stability by managing crises alone and controlling the narrative they receive, while telling herself she is being practical rather than protective.
candidates.explanation: E1: She invents 'Operation Manage' (L37-39) to hide the crisis from siblings, and tells Bisola a euphemism ('Daddy is changing business,' L41) she herself marks as untrue (L42: 'Which, you know'). She frames this as learning to prioritize material reality over emotion (L63-65: 'Not how do I feel about it'). E2: When her father has a health crisis, she deliberately avoids calling Aunty Funmi to prevent one year of being reminded of the debt (L39: 'every conversation will have that inside it'), even though she knows Aunty will send money and solve the problem faster. She solves it herself instead, using her allowance and her mother's hidden resources (L41-42: 'I took my whole allowance... My mummy sold — well. We sorted it'). The stated frame is pragmatism; the lived pattern is: she bears crises alone to protect others from obligation or shame. E4 repeats this: she does Mama Ronke's care beyond her duty (plaiting hair, talking to her) while saying 'Not for her, she didn't know. For me' (L28-29). The gap between stated and lived is: she says it is self-protective (I don't get attached, L48); it is actually family-protective (she is solving problems no one asked her to solve, and absorbing the cost).
candidates.narrator_frame: E1 L63-65: 'That year taught me to look at a situation and ask, what is the actual quantity remaining, and how many days. Not how do I feel about it.' E2 L57: 'It's like, when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand.'
candidates.form_evidence: Agency grammar shifts when she describes her own choices: 'I went,' 'I counted,' 'I told them' (E1), 'I called my coursemate,' 'I took my whole allowance' (E2), 'I was doing her mouth care' (E4). When she describes the cost, agency dissolves: 'she would send the money, yes... and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it' (E2 L39-40, passive construction). She uses precision (dates, quantities, durations) to manage situations but disclaims she is tracking ('not a person that keeps record,' E1 L52, contradicted immediately by L60-61: 'That's just how my head is. I know it was the 14th of September').
candidates.check: E1 (crisis management at 14: invents system, controls sibling narrative); E2 (father's health crisis at 19: avoids asking for help despite knowing it would solve faster); E4 (patient death at 23: care work beyond duty, frames as 'for me'); E5 (IELTS and emigration plan at 24: hidden from family, frames as 'can't bring it to the table'). Four of four experiences show her solving family problems alone and controlling information flow.

Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because the speaker waited until the crisis was resolved (L44: 'after he was stable and discharged, I called Aunty'). She controlled the timing and the narrative frame: she solved it first, then disclosed. She did not ask for help; she asked for retroactive validation. This is consistent with the pattern: she protects her family by solving alone, then manages the relational cost by controlling the story.

Agency grammar: active and precise when acting alone ('I counted,' 'I went,' 'I did the change of course myself'), passive or absent when her own needs appear ('It's like, when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand,' E2 L57-58).
candidates.check: E1 (age 14): takes on crisis management without telling anyone—belief fits. E2 (age 19): refuses to ask for help even though it will solve the problem faster, to avoid creating relational obligation—belief fits. E3 (age 17-18): tells the interviewer version of her nursing story, admits 'the honest version is not the version I give at interviews' (L1)—belief fits (she manages the narrative others receive). E5 (age 24): plans major life decision in complete secrecy with full cost analysis, will not disclose until 'already done' (L29)—belief fits. Four of five experiences show this mechanism.
candidates.counterexample: E2 L44-51: She calls Aunty Funmi and tells her what happened, and Aunty sends money. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because she only tells after solving the crisis ('after he was stable and discharged,' L44). She does not ask; she informs. The mechanism is not that she never tells—it is that she must solve alone first, then control the narrative frame of the telling. The belief permits disclosure only after the problem is managed, so the disclosure is not a request for help but a report of completed action.

evidence.quote: I knew what would happen — she would send the money, yes, she would absolutely send it, and then for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it. Every single one. So I called my coursemate Kemi.

I can't bring it to the table until I know. Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for. You understand? Five people are disappointed instead of one. When I have the CBT pass in my hand, then I'll say it. Maybe when I have the offer. I'll come and say, Mummy, this is what has been happening, and it is already done.

candidates.falsifier: She asks for help or discloses a plan before she has a solution or certainty, and feels relief rather than anxiety about doing so.
candidates.would_predict: Personal Growth: When she experiences a setback or failure in private (failed exam, rejected application, relationship ending), she will not disclose it to close family until she has 'fixed' it or has moved past it. If forced to disclose before she is ready, she will experience shame or a sense that she has burdened others, even if they express support.

candidates.headline: She excels at seeing a system's constraints, designing a structure that creates agency in others within those constraints, and executing it alone without external validation or permission.
candidates.explanation: E1: At 14, without being asked and without adult guidance, she enters a storage room, invents a taxonomy (Item, Quantity, Days to Depletion), calculates food consumption rates for seven people, and projects dates. Then she converts this data into a game ('Operation Manage') that turns scarcity into competition, creates a reward structure that requires no resources (choosing Sunday viewing), and makes her siblings active participants in managing the crisis. She is energized by this work ('something in my chest go down,' L34). E3: At 17, after failing to get medicine, she faces three paths (rewrite, change course, private university). Instead of choosing from the offered options, she invents a fourth path: she goes to a cyber café and changes her course to nursing herself, paying with her own money, telling no one (L42-44). She is solving a problem (unclear pathway to medicine) by recognizing that nursing offers what she actually needs: a transparent, steps-based structure ('when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything,' L41). E5: At 24, she plans emigration by: (1) working out the exact visa and licensing pathway from the NMC website, (2) calculating costs in three scenarios with currency fluctuation, (3) determining what salary she needs and where, (4) reverse-engineering a contribution plan for her siblings' education (L34-42: 'on a band 5 starting salary... I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month comfortably. Which handles Tayo completely and starts a pool for Bisola'). This is not daydreaming; it is systems design. The genius is: she sees constraints (no family capital, four siblings, uncertain income), and designs a structure that creates agency and distributes responsibility (if she earns, the siblings advance).
candidates.narrator_frame: E1 L34: 'writing it made something in my chest go down. Like when you finally find where the mosquito is hiding.' E3 L41: 'when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything.' E5 L12-16: 'I opened the NMC website and I wrote out the whole thing in my book. CBT, then application, then qualification verification, then OSCE... I did three columns. Best case, medium, worst. I even put a column for if the pound moves.'
candidates.form_evidence: Specificity explosion when she is designing or executing systems: E1 lists book type ('Olympic 40-leaves'), taxonomic categories ('Item, Quantity, How many days it can carry us'), consumption rates ('rice three times a week'). E3: 'the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel' (L39). E5: three-column cost model with currency variables, salary calculations after tax and rent, regional choice (Midlands not London because of cost, L40). When she is NOT designing, specificity collapses into metaphor or absence: E2 L45-60 (describing emotional cost of Aunty's support, she uses metaphor 'like, when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand' instead of naming the feeling). Precision is deployed for structure, not introspection.
candidates.check: E1 (age 14): invents inventory system, converts to game, executes unprompted—genius visible. E2 (age 19): no system design visible—genius not active in this domain (medical crisis). E3 (age 17-18): sees nursing as transparent pathway, researches handbook as 'novel,' executes course change alone—genius visible. E4 (age 23): follows protocol for last offices ('there is an order, first this, then this,' L44), executes protocol with precision, but this is following structure not designing it—genius not primary here. E5 (age 24): three-scenario cost model, salary-based contribution plan, NMC pathway mapping—genius visible. Four of five experiences show this pattern; in E2 and E4 the genius is not activated (medical crisis is not a systems design problem; clinical protocol is given, not invented).
candidates.counterexample: E4 L32-36: Sister Adaeze tells her 'you're doing too much, this is not your patient alone, you have six others' (L32). The speaker says 'yes ma. I didn't stop' (L35-36). This could suggest she is not actually solving a system problem; she is just over-identifying with a patient. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because E4 is not a systems design story; it is a care story. Her genius activates when there is a constraint-and-structure problem to solve (How do we eat during financial crisis? How do I access medicine with no contacts? How do I pay for my siblings' school from abroad?). Mama Ronke's care does not present a systems problem—it presents an emotional one. She resists solving it ('I didn't stop') but this is NOT her genius zone; this is a collision between her genius (structure) and her care for others (affect).

evidence.quote: I told them we were doing a competition. I called it Operation Manage. Whoever wastes the least food in a week gets to choose what we watch on Sunday.

When I got the handbook in first year and I saw the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel. My roommate was laughing at me. But you know what that is, that's — when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything.

candidates.falsifier: She asks someone else to design the system, or she freezes and takes no action when confronted with a constraint-based problem.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career: In a role with undefined structure or processes, she will quickly map the constraints and design a system (workflow, resource allocation, communication structure) without being asked. She will implement it and others will recognize it as elegant. She may not receive credit for this work, and she may not seek it, but she will become the person others 'ask how to do things.' Possible blind spot: she may assume others can see and use the system as easily as she designed it, and become frustrated with slow adoption or misuse.

candidates.headline: She maintains precise, indexed memories of others' behaviour (dates, durations, specific words, objects), while simultaneously disclaiming she is tracking, and this data appears to function as a measure of whether others showed up for her.
candidates.explanation: E1: She states 'I am not a person that keeps record of what people did' (L52), then immediately contradicts this: 'That's just how my head is' (L60), and provides precise indexing: Uncle Segun came 'September and then just before Christmas,' and the first visit was 'the 14th of September because it was after my birthday' (L54, L61). She recalls the car negotiation as exactly 'one hour twenty minutes' (L47). She knows generator brands and can 'spell demurrage backwards' (L11). E4: She states 'I don't get attached, that's the thing about me, I think I'm actually quite hard in that way' (L48), yet she remembers the son's shoes ('nice shoes, I remember the shoes because they were the kind that makes that sound on the floor,' L7) and recalls he did not visit for 'nineteen days' (L14-15, repeated: 'I know it was nineteen because I know,' L17). She carries Mama Ronke's comb in her bag 'since last year' (L50-52), meaning she has kept an object from a deceased patient. She tells the son 'she was comfortable,' but also notes 'I will tell you that I remember what date he last came before that, and I remember what the shoes sounded like' (L60). The pattern: she collects precise data about who showed up, when, and what they brought (or didn't). She measures her own value through this data, then denies she is doing so. Question: Does she believe that if she acknowledges she is tracking loyalty, she is admitting she is keeping score (which feels disloyal)? Or does the tracking feel like the only form of witnessing available to her?
candidates.narrator_frame: E1 L52: 'I am not a person that keeps record of what people did.' Directly contradicted by L60-61: 'That's just how my head is. I know it was the 14th of September.' E4 L48: 'I don't get attached.' Contradicted by L50-52: 'Her comb is in my bag. The small black one. It's been there since last year.'
candidates.form_evidence: Precision asymmetry: She is exact about when others appeared or failed to appear (Uncle Segun: September + December, dated to L61's 14th September; Mama Ronke's son: 19 days absent; the car buyer: 1 hour 20 minutes of haggling). She is vague about her own emotional response to these absences (E1 L52: 'I'm not saying anything... I'm not holding anything' trails off without answering). Specificity collapses when she names her own stake in the data: E1 L56-58: 'I greet them well. When Uncle Kunle's daughter was doing her wedding introduction last year I was the one that did the small chops arrangement, I didn't even collect money. So it's not that I'm holding anything.' This is performative disproof of the tracking she just did. Agency grammar: when she is being tracked (by Aunty Funmi's requirements, by the absence of Mama Ronke's son), she uses passive or constrained language ('the conditions were never written down but everybody knows them,' E2 L24); when she is tracking others, she uses active, precise language ('I know,' 'I remember,' 'I was watching from the window,' E1 L48).
candidates.check: E1: precise dates and durations for uncle visits; precise inventory of generator brands, book type, consumption calculations. Disclaims tracking ('not a person that keeps record'). E4: precise timeline (19 days), sensory detail (shoe sound), object retention (comb in bag). Disclaims attachment ('I don't get attached'). Both instances show: precise data + disclaimer of keeping score. E2 and E3 do not foreground this pattern (E2 is about relational debt, E3 about decision-making). E5 does not foreground it. So: present in two of five experiences, both explicitly contradicted by disclaimer.
candidates.counterexample: E1 L56-58: She says 'I greet them well' and 'I was the one that did the small chops arrangement, I didn't even collect money. So it's not that I'm holding anything.' This could suggest she is NOT measuring loyalty; she is performing generosity toward people who disappeared. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because the very existence of this disclaimer proves she is aware she is measuring. She is explicitly disproving a charge no one made. The fact that she performs generosity toward the aunts and uncles who did not show up during the crisis suggests she experiences her own tracking as a form of judgment she must actively disprove. The pattern is: she tracks, then performs generosity to prove she is not tracking, then denies she tracks. This is triple negation.

evidence.quote: The only one that came to the house that whole time was Uncle Segun, and he came twice, September and then just before Christmas, and the second time he brought a bag of rice and a crate of egg and he didn't even come inside, he dropped it at the gate.

candidates.falsifier: She acknowledges she is tracking others' behaviour and uses it to assess their care for her, and feels comfortable naming this as a legitimate form of self-protection.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: In a close relationship, she will notice and remember small failures to show up or follow through (partner forgetting a detail she mentioned, late arrival, missed call) and will accumulate these into a data set she does not name. When the relationship ends or cracks, she will produce this data as evidence of neglect, and the other person will be shocked because the data was never surfaced. She may experience herself as 'just stating facts' while the other person experiences her as 'keeping score.'

candidates.headline: She describes herself as analytical and pragmatic, but her major decisions emerge from bodily knowing or ambient cues, executed first and rationalized after.
candidates.explanation: E3: She is deciding between rewriting JAMB, changing courses, or paying for private medicine school. This is a high-stakes, rational decision. But she states explicitly: 'I didn't reason it. I want to be clear, there was no reasoning. It was like somebody came and put it in my hand' (L29-31). The trigger: watching a woman sell gala in the rain with wet hands. 'My mind just — it went quiet. And I said, nursing. Just like that... The rain hadn't even stopped. I didn't reason it' (L24-29). Then after: 'Then after, I built all the reasons. Oh, nursing is four to five years not seven. Oh, nursing you can travel with it...' (L32-38). This is post-hoc rationalization. She describes her decision-making style to others as analytical ('I tell them I'm a very analytical person,' L59), but the actual pattern is: her body/intuition decides, her mind catches up. E5: She is making a second major decision (emigration, hidden from family). She says: 'I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it' (L52-53). She has done three-scenario cost analysis and NMC pathway research, but the final decision will not be rational. It will emerge from her body/situation, as with nursing. She frames this as involuntary ('my mouth will say it'), not chosen. The lived pattern: bodily knowing first, rationalization second. The stated frame: 'I'm a very analytical person.'
candidates.narrator_frame: E3 L59: 'I tell them I'm a very analytical person.' Contradicted by L29-31: 'I didn't reason it. I want to be clear, there was no reasoning. It was like somebody came and put it in my hand.' E5 L52-53: 'I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it.'
candidates.form_evidence: Temporal grammar shifts: when describing the nursing decision, she uses past perfect for rationalization ('I built all the reasons,' E3 L32) but simple past for the felt decision ('I said, nursing. Just like that,' L25-26). The rationalization is constructed; the decision is reported as given. She describes the construction process as a separate event ('Then after, I built all the reasons'). Same pattern in E5: the analysis is detailed and time-stamped ('In February I wrote IELTS,' 'I opened the NMC website,' 'I did three columns'), but the final decision-point is not. She has not decided whether to go; she is waiting for her body to tell her. Specificity collapses at the decision-point: she can calculate cost to the pound, but cannot say 'I will emigrate' or 'I will not.' Instead: 'I'll probably know when I know... my mouth will say it' (E5 L52-53). She delegates agency to her body.
candidates.check: E1 (age 14): Creates inventory system. She says 'I don't even know why I did it, nobody sent me' (L25). This is bodily; then she reflects on why it was useful. E3 (age 17-18): Nursing decision driven by watching a woman in rain; rationalized after. E4 (age 23): Care work with Mama Ronke driven by feeling ('it was disturbing me,' L28) not protocol. E5 (age 24): Major emigration decision will emerge from bodily knowing ('my mouth will say it'), despite detailed analysis. Four of five experiences show this pattern: bodily knowing or ambient sensing, rationalization after.
candidates.counterexample: E5 L12-16: She does detailed analysis—three-column cost model, salary calculations, NMC pathway mapping, currency variables. This looks analytical and first. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because the analysis is means-finding, not decision-making. She has already decided (bodily) to pursue this; the analysis is mapping the path to execute that decision. She is not analyzing whether to go; she is analyzing how. The decision-point (go or stay) will not be rational. She says so explicitly: 'I don't know if I'll go... I'll probably know when I know' (E5 L48-52). The analysis is in service of a decision that has not yet arrived.

evidence.quote: Some days I'm reading the NMC page and I'm calm, everything is steps, do step one do step two. Other days I'm thinking, if I leave, who is the one that will be at the house when my daddy's BP does that thing again. Who will count what is remaining. I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it.
That's how most of my big things have gone, if I'm honest. Which I don't tell people because it sounds mad. I tell them I'm a very analytical person.

candidates.falsifier: She describes a major decision (nursing, emigration, or earlier choice) where she reasoned through options systematically first, then acted on that reasoning.
candidates.would_predict: Personal Growth: When she is stuck on a decision, deliberately trying to think her way through it (should I stay in Nigeria or go, should I specialize in this area or that), analysis will stall her. She is more likely to find clarity through situations that trigger bodily response (walking, crisis, ambient sensing). If she trusts her analytical mind as her primary decision-making tool, she will experience recurring cycles of overthinking without resolution, until something forces a choice.

candidates.headline: By E5, she has moved from absorbing her family's crisis (inventory at 14) to pre-emptively planning to become her family's solution (emigration plan at 24), and the logic suggests she may not believe there is an alternative.
candidates.explanation: E1 (age 14): Crisis arrives; she responds by counting, organizing, managing her siblings' knowledge. She is reactive but extraordinary at it. E2 (age 19): Someone else (Aunty Funmi) is the primary financial solution; she resists becoming dependent on that role. E3 (age 17-18): She commits to nursing, a path that 'has a licence with a number,' transparency, predictability. It is also a care profession. E4 (age 23): In clinical work, she performs care labor beyond duty (plaiting hair, mouth care, talking to a dead patient), despite Sister Adaeze telling her she is doing too much. E5 (age 24): She has worked out that on a UK nurse salary, 'I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month comfortably. Which handles Tayo completely and starts a pool for Bisola' (L40-41). She is not emigrating for herself; she is emigrating to become the financial solution for her four siblings. She states: 'That's the whole thing. That's the actual reason' (L42-43). The compounding insight: she has internalized the role of crisis-absorber (E1), refused to be a dependent (E2), chosen a profession structured around care (E3), practiced it beyond what is required (E4), and now is planning to sacrifice geographic proximity and her own life preference ('I like Lagos,' 'I like that I can hear my mummy from the kitchen,' E5 L46-47) to fund her siblings' education. The logic is internally consistent: if I am the one who manages, I must become the one who solves. This is only visible once all five experiences are in because E5 shows the trajectory completing—she is not just managing a crisis, she is building her life around preventing future crises for her family.
candidates.narrator_frame: E5 L42-43: 'That's the whole thing. That's the actual reason.' Also L46-47: 'I like Lagos. I like that I can hear my mummy from the kitchen.' And L48-50: 'I don't know if I'll go... if I leave, who is the one that will be at the house when my daddy's BP does that thing again. Who will count what is remaining.'
candidates.form_evidence: Escalation in sacrifice: E1 (psychological labor, sibling management); E2 (emotional labor, refusing to ask for help); E3 (career sacrifice, giving up medicine for nursing); E4 (bodily labor, care beyond duty); E5 (geographic and relational sacrifice, emigration to fund siblings). The logic is: someone must solve this. The logic compounds: that someone has to be me. The form evidence is the progression of the same gesture (managing, solving, absorbing) across different domains. By E5, she is not just reacting to crisis; she is pre-designing a life structure around preventing family crisis.
candidates.check: E1: reactive crisis management (inventory, game). E2: resistance to dependency (solving the medical crisis herself). E3: choice of structured care profession. E4: excessive care work (plaiting hair, night shifts). E5: prospective life design to solve future crises (emigration plan). Each experience deepens the pattern; by E5 the pattern has become proactive and architectured.
candidates.counterexample: None found. Every experience shows escalating assumption of family-problem responsibility. E2 comes closest: she refuses to call Aunty Funmi, suggesting she resists the role of dependent. But she does not refuse the role of problem-solver; she just solves it herself. This is consistent with the compounding pattern, not contrary to it.

evidence.quote: I was turning her two-hourly with whoever I could grab. I plaited her hair one night because it was matting and I couldn't — it was disturbing me. Not for her, she didn't know. For me.

candidates.falsifier: She names a point in her life where she chose not to solve a family problem, or where she let the problem remain unsolved, or where she named that this is not her responsibility.
candidates.would_predict: Purpose: If this emigration plan succeeds (visa, job, sponsorship), she will experience it not as freedom or personal achievement, but as responsibility. She will send money. She will also experience recurrent anxiety about what is happening at home without her. She will not 'move abroad' in the sense of building a life there; she will build a life structured around remote family management. The dark version of this prediction: she will burn out, or she will achieve all the external markers of success (UK residency, licensed nurse, income) while experiencing profound emptiness or resentment, because she moved abroad to solve a problem but the problem (her parents' precarity, her siblings' dependence) cannot be solved by individual earning.

candidates.headline: She believes that if a system or path is transparent and rule-based (you do step one, step two, step three and you arrive), then she can navigate it alone and without dependency.
candidates.explanation: E1: She is facing a financial crisis with no transparent outcome. She invents transparency: 'Item, Quantity, How many days it can carry us' (L27-29). This makes the crisis predictable and manageable. E3: She faced three opaque paths to medicine (rewrite, change course, private university)—all involving gatekeeping and 'knowing somebody.' Nursing offers a different kind of path: 'you do your programme, you do your indexing, you register with the Nursing and Midwifery Council, you have a licence with a number. There is a syllabus. Nobody can come and say ah your uncle knows so-and-so' (L35-37). This is the actual reason she chose it, though she told interviewers it was inspiration from her grandmother's nurse. She states: 'when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything' (L41). E4: In clinical work, there is a transparent protocol for last offices: 'there is an order. First this, then this' (L44-45). She executes it with precision and steadiness. E5: She maps the entire emigration pathway step by step: 'CBT, then application, then qualification verification, then OSCE, then the OSCE is in the UK so you need the visa, which means you need the job offer, which means the sponsorship' (L12-13). She does this work in columns (best case, medium, worst). This belief permits her to navigate systems alone because she does not need to ask anyone or know anyone; she just needs to see the steps. This is why she can act alone: the system is the permission.
candidates.narrator_frame: E3 L35-41: 'In nursing your progression is written down — you do your programme, you do your indexing, you register with the Nursing and Midwifery Council, you have a licence with a number. There is a syllabus. Nobody can come and say ah your uncle knows so-and-so. I actually liked that a lot. When I got the handbook in first year and I saw the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel... when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything.'
candidates.form_evidence: Specificity explosion when describing or designing transparent systems: E1 (Item, Quantity, Days to Depletion, consumption rate, depletion date); E3 (handbook as 'whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours,' read 'like a novel'); E4 (protocol for last offices: 'wash the body, position it, pack with cotton wool, remove the cannula and the catheter, do the identification, write the tag, record the time on the chart,' L43). E5 (three-column cost model with currency variable, NMC pathway as linked conditionals: 'visa... means... sponsorship'). When the path is opaque (whether to go to UK or stay), specificity collapses and she defers to bodily knowing ('I'll probably know when I know'). The belief licenses her to act alone: opaque paths require relationship/permission; transparent paths she can execute solo.
candidates.check: E1: invents transparency in crisis (inventory = structure). E2: not primarily about systems (about relational debt). E3: chooses a profession specifically for pathway transparency; researches handbook obsessively. E4: finds peace in protocol (last offices). E5: maps entire emigration pathway; three scenarios. Four of five experiences show this pattern; E2 is relational not systemic. When the path becomes opaque (stay or go, E5 L48-52), she stalls and waits for bodily knowing.
candidates.counterexample: E2 L24-30: Aunty Funmi's support has unwritten conditions ('The conditions were never written down but everybody knows them. I call her every Sunday evening... I send my results, photographed, every semester...'). This is an opaque, relational system that she must navigate through compliance, not transparent rules. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because she experiences this system as constraining and unstable (L57-60: 'when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand'). She is trying to navigate an opaque system and it is costing her. This is evidence for the belief: transparent systems free her; opaque systems constrain her.

evidence.quote: When we did the last offices, Sister Adaeze took me through it. And there is a way you do it. You wash the body, you position it, you pack with cotton wool, you remove the cannula and the catheter, you do the identification, you write the tag, you record the time on the chart. There is an order. First this, then this.

I opened the NMC website and I wrote out the whole thing in my book. CBT, then application, then qualification verification, then OSCE, then the OSCE is in the UK so you need the visa, which means you need the job offer, which means the sponsorship...

candidates.falsifier: She navigates an opaque, relational system successfully, or she feels free and capable within a system where the rules are unwritten and dependent on personal relationships.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career: She will gravitate toward roles and institutions with clear hierarchies, written protocols, and transparent progression (healthcare, civil service, military, structured finance). She will excel in these contexts. She may struggle in roles requiring political navigation, relationship-building, or informal influence. She may experience workplaces with 'organic culture' or 'you have to know people' as exhausting or threatening. She will document and systematize processes others leave informal.

candidates.headline: Across all five experiences, she does not appear as a subject wanting something for herself; she appears as a function responding to a situation or serving others.
candidates.explanation: E1 (age 14): The experience is her response to financial crisis, not her own adolescence. No mention of friends, crushes, school interests, what she wanted. School appears only as the venue for greeting her father (L23). Her own affect appears only once, as relief at solving the problem (L34). E2 (age 19): She enters nursing school on Aunty's money. The experience is Aunty's generosity and the conditions attached; her own motivation for nursing is absent. (That comes in E3, where she confesses the real reason, not in E2.) E3 (age 17-18): She wants medicine, fails to get it, then decides nursing at Ojota under rain. But her own experience of the decision is reported as non-agentive ('like somebody came and put it in my hand,' L31; 'it was just the moment my body decided something,' L56). She does not say 'I chose nursing' but 'nursing was chosen in me.' E4 (age 23): She is a nurse doing care work. Her own interiority—whether she is fulfilled, whether she wants to be there, what she wants from this work—is not present. She talks about the work and the patient; she does not talk about herself. E5 (age 24): She is planning emigration. But it is framed not as her life but as her siblings' solution. 'The real calculation is Tayo... I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month. Which handles Tayo completely' (L34-41). She states: 'I like Lagos. I like that I can hear my mummy from the kitchen' (L46-47), but immediately: 'And honestly I don't know if I'll go' (L48). Her own desire and her own life are marked as contingent, maybe, provisional. Across all five experiences, she does not have a first-person narrative about what she wants to become or what would fulfill her.
candidates.narrator_frame: E3 L59: 'I tell them I'm a very analytical person.' This is the only place she describes herself as a person with attributes. Otherwise, she describes herself as a responder. E5 L55-57: 'I'm not even a person who thinks about myself like this, my friends will tell you I don't like all this deep-deep conversation. Let me go and read, jare.' She is explaining why talking about herself feels wrong to her.
candidates.form_evidence: Absence of first-person want-states ('I want X,' 'I love Y,' 'I am interested in Z') across the corpus, except in E5 L46-47 ('I like Lagos, I like that I can hear my mummy from the kitchen'), which is immediately undercut ('And honestly I don't know if I'll go,' L48). When she speaks about her own preferences or emotions, they are framed as already decided for her (E3: 'I didn't reason it,' 'like somebody came and put it in my hand'; E5: 'I'll probably know when I know... my mouth will say it'). She speaks about herself in terms of function ('I don't get attached,' E4 L48; 'I'm a very analytical person,' E3 L59) rather than values or desires. The absence is structural: she is absent as a subject with her own trajectory.

insights.headline: She protects her family's functional stability by solving crises alone and controlling the narrative they receive, while framing this as pragmatism rather than protection.
insights.explanation: E1: At 14, during financial collapse, she invents an inventory system and game ('Operation Manage') without being asked, managing her siblings' knowledge. She tells Bisola a euphemism ('Daddy is changing business') she marks as untrue (L42: 'Which, you know'). Stated frame: learning to prioritize material reality (L63-65: 'Not how do I feel about it'). Lived pattern: she solves problems alone to protect others from knowledge or obligation. E2: When her father is acutely ill, she avoids calling Aunty Funmi—who would solve fastest—because she knows it creates one year of relational debt (L39: 'every conversation will have that inside it'). She solves it herself instead, using her allowance and her mother's hidden resources (L41-42). E5: She plans emigration in secret (L17: 'I have not told one single person in my family'), controlling when and how her family learns about it. Why? 'the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for' (L24-25). The gap: she says she is pragmatic; she is actually bearing family crises alone to protect others from shame or burden.
insights.narrator_frame: E1 L63-65: 'That year taught me to look at a situation and ask, what is the actual quantity remaining, and how many days. Not how do I feel about it.' E5 L24-26: 'Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for.'
insights.form_evidence: Active, precise agency when solving alone ('I went,' 'I counted,' 'I called my coursemate,' 'I took my whole allowance'). When describing the cost of accepting help, agency becomes constrained or passive ('she would send... and then for the next one year'). She uses dates, quantities, durations to manage situations but disclaims she is tracking ('not a person that keeps record,' E1 L52, contradicted by L60-61).

The behaviour implies: her distress would add to her parents' distress, so she protects by managing silently. E2 (age 19): When her father is acutely ill, she deliberately avoids calling Aunty Funmi because the money will create relational debt ('for the next one year every conversation will have that inside it,' L39-40). The belief: if I ask for help, I become a problem someone else has to solve. E5 (age 24): She plans emigration in complete secrecy, calculating costs in three scenarios (L12-16). 'Because the moment I say it, it becomes a thing that everybody is holding, and then if it doesn't work, I'm not the only one that it didn't work for' (L24-26). When her own needs surface: passive or metaphorical ('It's like, when somebody is holding you up, you start to walk in a way that doesn't disturb their hand,' E2 L57-58). insights.headline: She excels at seeing a system's constraints, designing structures that create agency in others within those constraints, and executing the solution alone without external validation.
insights.explanation: E1 (age 14): Without being asked, she enters a storage room, invents a taxonomy (Item, Quantity, Days to Depletion), calculates food consumption for seven people, and projects depletion dates. She then converts this data into a game ('Operation Manage') that makes her siblings active participants in scarcity management without external resources (the reward is choosing Sunday viewing, which requires no cost). She is energized by this work ('something in my chest go down,' L34). E3 (age 17-18): After failing medicine, she recognizes that nursing offers transparent structure ('when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything,' L41). She goes to a cyber café and changes her course herself, paying with her own money, telling no one (L42-44). E5 (age 24): She works out the exact visa and licensing pathway from the NMC website, calculates costs in three scenarios with currency fluctuation, determines the salary she needs, and reverse-engineers a contribution plan: 'I can send maybe six, seven hundred pounds a month comfortably. Which handles Tayo completely and starts a pool for Bisola' (L40-41). This is not daydreaming; it is systems design that creates agency for her siblings through her own structure.

E3 L41: 'when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything.' E5 L12-16: 'I opened the NMC website and I wrote out the whole thing in my book... I did three columns. Best case, medium, worst.'
insights.form_evidence: Specificity explosion when designing systems: book type ('Olympic 40-leaves'), taxonomic categories ('Item, Quantity, How many days'), consumption rates ('rice three times a week'). E3: 'the whole four years laid out, courses, clinical postings, hours, I read it like a novel' (L39). E5: three-column cost model, salary calculations after tax and rent, regional choice (Midlands, not London). Precision is deployed for structure-design, not introspection.

E3 (age 17-18): sees nursing as transparent pathway, executes course change alone—genius visible. E5 (age 24): three-scenario cost model, contribution plan—genius visible. Three of five experiences show this pattern activated.
insights.counterexample: E4 L32-36: Sister Adaeze says 'you're doing too much, this is not your patient alone, you have six others.' The speaker says 'yes ma. I didn't stop' (L35-36). This could suggest she is over-identifying with a patient rather than solving a system problem. Why doesn't this defeat the claim? Because E4 is a care story, not a systems design story. Her genius activates when there is a constraint-and-structure problem to solve (financial crisis, unclear pathway, emigration cost). Mama Ronke's care presents an emotional problem, not a systems one. This is a collision between her genius (structure) and her care for others (affect), not evidence against genius.
